1:
Gill glosses the voice briefly, as heard in the law and by the prophets. Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as a heading rather than a promise: the thought with which the discourse on the law had just terminated forms the theme, and in a certain sense the title, of the whole description that follows, and the indispensable condition of obtaining the blessing is obedience — a condition Moses is so anxious to impress that he repeats it at the commencement, again in the middle of the list, and again at its close. Clarke does the same work another way, opening with the argument of the chapter: the blessings on the obedient, the privileges of the faithful, the curses on the idolatrous, and the long account of the miseries, ending with the scattering among all the nations.

Henry reads the order itself as doctrine. The blessings are put before the curses to intimate that God is slow to anger but swift to show mercy, that he had said and sworn he would much rather we obeyed and lived than sinned and died, and that it is his delight to bless. Though both promises and threatenings are designed to hold us to our duty, it is better that we be allured to good by a filial hope of God's favour than frightened to it by a servile fear of his wrath; the obedience that pleases best comes from a principle of delight in God's goodness. He sets out the conditions in three: that they diligently hearken, using their utmost endeavours to acquaint themselves with God's will; that they observe and do all the commandments and keep them, not doing them for once but for ever, not merely setting out in God's ways but walking in them to the end; and that they turn aside neither to the right hand nor the left, to superstition on the one hand or profaneness on the other, and above all not after other gods, the sin they were most prone to and God most displeased with.

Ellicott takes the promise literally and finds a divine name in it: the Lord will make thee Most High, the very word used of God himself. He gathers the parallels where a name of God is laid on a people or a place — Jerusalem called Jehovah-Tzidkenu, the city named Jehovah-Shammah, the promise to write on the overcomer the name of God and of the city of God, and the servants who have his Name in their foreheads. Calvin reads the same clause as pre-eminence rather than title: the diversity of expression and the repetition alike tend to confirmation, and what is meant is that God would deal so bountifully with them that they should be illustrious above all the rest of the world.

What Calvin then draws from the catalogue is not its grandeur but its length. The enumeration reminds us not only in how many ways God is bountiful towards his servants, but also to how many necessities we are exposed, which require his direct and constant aid; for if we are blessed in the city and in the field, we can no more move a foot than stand still except by his blessing. Such is the tendency of the whole list: a scarcity of all things impends over us at every moment unless God continually succour us by remedies sent down from heaven, every good thing coming only from that one source. Henry sees the same abundance from the other side and fastens on the word overtake: good people, under a sense of their own unworthiness, are sometimes ready to fly from the blessing and conclude it does not belong to them, but the blessing shall find them out and follow them notwithstanding — as in the great day it will overtake the righteous who ask when they ever saw the Lord hungry and fed him.
2:
The word all four of them stop on is overtake. Gill has the blessings come from God out of heaven by the direction of his providence, freely and plentifully, beyond their expectations and deserts, and continue with them. Wesley puts it as a reversal of the world's usual chase: those blessings which others greedily follow after and never overtake shall follow after thee, and be thrown into thy lap by special kindness. Ellicott calls it a beautiful expression, meaning that the blessing shall come home and impress the heart with the thought of God's love and his promises when it is least expected, and cites the prophet's question whether God's words and statutes did not take hold of — that is, overtake — the fathers, so that they turned and said that as the Lord of hosts thought to do to them, so had he dealt with them; and he notes that the same is true in the other direction of the curses.

Clarke takes the image as a journey and hangs four observations on it. The voice of God must be heard, for without a divine revelation how can the divine will be known, and if not known it cannot be fulfilled. When God speaks men must hearken to the words of his mouth, since he who does not hearken will not obey. He who hearkens must set out for the kingdom of heaven, the curse falling on the man who stands in the way of sinners and overtaking those who loiter in the way of righteousness. And those who run in the way of God's testimonies shall have abundance of blessing, receiving in every part of their march through life the fulfilment of the various promises that relate to all circumstances and stages of it, each overtaking them in the time and place where it is most needed. Keil and Delitzsch read the structure instead, and mark that the verses following describe the effect of the blessing on every situation the nation might be placed in — its attitude towards its enemies, its trade and handicraft, and its standing among all the nations of the earth.

On the city and the field the glosses are short and go two ways. Clarke divides them by occupation, the city meaning all civil employments and the field all agricultural pursuits, and Wesley says the same of husbandmen and tradesmen, town and country, who should be preserved from the dangers of both and have the comforts of both — from which he takes the lesson that we must depend on God constantly, needing him at every turn, since we cannot be safe if he withdraw his protection nor easy if he suspend his favour, but if he bless us it is well with us wherever we go. Gill fills the city in with detail: not only Jerusalem, where the temple would be built and they would be blessed with the service and ordinances of God, but all the other cities of the land, where they should dwell in large and spacious houses, their cities walled and fenced and very populous, enjoying health and plenty of provisions and prospering in all kinds of merchandise there, as Aben Ezra notes.

Of the fruit of the body Gill promises children many and living, healthful and thriving, arriving at manhood and perpetuating their families; and he passes on Grotius' opinion that the promise was eminently fulfilled in Mary, the mother of our Lord. Clarke keeps to the plain sense — all thy children — and extends the last clause as far as it will go, every animal employed in domestic and agricultural purposes being under the especial protection of Divine Providence.
5:
What the basket and the store were is the one real dispute here. Gill notes that the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem restrain the basket to the basket of firstfruits and the cake of the first of the dough, but takes it himself for every vessel in which provisions for present use are put, which should never be empty; Wesley reads the store as a storehouse, always well replenished and its provision preserved for use. Ellicott sets out how far the versions part. The word rendered store is identical in form with the word for kneading troughs, and all the Targums, all the Jewish commentators he could consult, and the lexicons take the contrast that way — either between firstfruits in their natural state and the dough already prepared, as in the wave-loaves, or between the vessel carrying the corn and the receptacle for the meal, or, as Rashi has it, between the vessel for things moist and the vessel for things dry. Against all of them Ellicott prefers the Septuagint's reading, that the basket is the portion brought out for the present occasion and the store what is left and put away for future use, because that view is as old as any and the contrast it gives is simpler and more comprehensive than one drawn from the details of the law.

Clarke goes a third way, and at length. He glosses the basket as the olive gathering and vintage, that being what such baskets collected, and the store as the kneading-trough or remainder, all laid up for future use as well as what is prepared for present consumption; some, he adds, take the one for property abroad and the other for all they have at home. Then he passes on Harmer's proposal. Commentators are at a loss why Moses, who elsewhere speaks in generals, should here be so minute as to name baskets, and those who explain either word of the repositories of corn forget that the barns are spoken of presently afterwards; so Harmer suggests that the basket means the travelling basket and the other word the leathern bag, both used for carrying things on a journey. The one word occurs nowhere else except in the account of the conveyance in which the firstfruits were carried to Jerusalem, the other nowhere but in the hurried journey out of Egypt, where it means the utensils in which the dough was carried, a piece of leather drawn together by rings. Hasselquist reports that the eastern people use baskets in travelling, made of the leaves of the date palm, a kind of short bag used in Turkey on journeys; and as meal, figs and raisins are still carried in a goat's skin in Barbary for a viaticum, so merchandise might anciently have been carried, and particularly the honey, oil and balm of Ezekiel. Sir J. Chardin supposed the same of the balm and honey Jacob sent into Egypt. Understood so, the passage promises Israel success in commerce, as the next promises personal safety in going out and returning.

Of that going out and coming in the notes are brief and one of them reaches further than the rest. Gill takes it of all business and employments, within doors or without, in every office public or private, in journeys, and particularly in going out to war and returning. Clarke divides it neatly: coming in from thy employment, thou shalt find no evil has happened to the family in thy absence; going out, thy way shall be made prosperous. Ellicott allows the details of life but sees a further meaning, the coming in of Christ being his entrance into this world's labour and his going out his departure; and he quotes Rashi, that thy departure from the world shall be like thine entrance into it, sinless — adding that the Jews as a whole do not believe in original sin.
7:
On the rout of the enemies the three agree, and differ only in what they illustrate it from. Gill names the nations it happened to — Philistines, Moabites, Syrians, Edomites and Ammonites, especially in the days of David. Clarke reads the verse as a promise of security against foreign invasion, or of the total discomfiture of the invaders should they enter the land: they come one way, in the firmest and most united manner, and flee seven ways, utterly broken, confounded and finally routed. Ellicott quotes Rashi for the manner of it, that such is the custom of them that are terrified, to scatter in every direction, and points to two histories where exactly that happened — the Midianites breaking before Gideon, and the Syrians abandoning their camp overnight.

The storehouses draw out a distinction our English hides. Gill takes them for barns, granaries and cellar, where corn, wine and oil were laid up, and makes the benefit a preservative one: the grain kept from vermin, the casks from bursting and running out. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause as a wish rather than a prediction — may the Lord command the blessing with thee, that is, put it at thy disposal, in thy granaries and store-rooms and in all thy business — and gloss the idiom of setting the hand as whatever a man undertakes. Ellicott observes that the noun occurs only here and in the proverb about honouring the Lord with one's substance and the firstfruits of all one's increase, so that the barns shall be filled with plenty and the presses burst out with new wine. In it he finds the same antithesis he had drawn from the basket and the store: the gathering in against the putting forth of the hand, revenue and expenditure alike prospered, a contrast plain in the Hebrew words though lost in ours. The closing promise he reads as something beyond abundance — fixity of tenure in the divine inheritance, a settled title to the land itself.

Clarke fastens instead on the verb, and gets a doctrine out of it. That the Lord shall command the blessing means everything a man has comes by divine appointment, and that he shall receive nothing casually or by accident, but each thing, spiritual and temporal alike, at the immediate order of God.
9:
Establish is the word they weigh. Gill takes it of continuance and settlement: having separated them from all others for his service, honour and glory, God would keep them such, settle them in the land, and confirm their privileges natural, civil and religious — and he notes the Targum of Jonathan's reading, that the Word of the Lord shall establish thee, he that brought them out of Egypt through the Red sea and the wilderness. Wesley says the same more shortly, that God would confirm the covenant by which he had separated them to himself as a holy and peculiar people. Ellicott traces the Hebrew instead, and finds the promise means either to maintain them in that position or to raise them up into it and exalt them to it in the fullest sense; the word, he adds, has branched into two lines of thought, taking the sense of permanence and perpetuity in Jewish literature, and through the Septuagint's rendering giving birth to the New Testament word for resurrection.

Keil and Delitzsch look backwards for the oath. The Lord had called Israel a holy nation when he concluded the covenant with it, and the words as he hath sworn unto thee point back to that promise, which is called an oath because it rested on the promises given to the patriarchs on oath and was contained implicitly in them. What he would now do is make the holiness and glory of Israel so clearly manifest that all nations should see that the name of the Lord is named upon it — the name of the Lord being the revelation of his glorious nature, and named upon Israel when Israel is transformed into the glory of that nature. Clarke reduces the whole verse to one sentence and one warning: this is the sum of all blessings, to be made holy and preserved in holiness; and here is the solemn condition, that if they did not keep God's testimonies as the regulators of their lives, the curses and not the blessings must be their portion.

Calvin will not let the earthly reading stand alone. The promise does refer to earthly blessings, as though Moses said that by them God's love towards his chosen people would be manifested, and yet it rises higher, so that the Israelites, led on by degrees, should learn to embrace God alone and to trust in him according to the covenant made with Abraham — I am thy exceeding great reward. The children of Abraham were set apart to be a holy people not merely in order that, being well fed and with a full belly, they should aspire to nothing but earthly things, but that they might be confidently assured they would be blessed in death as well as in life. Their adoption was gratuitous, yet since they were called unto purity it is not without reason that God promises that what he had spoken should be sure if by keeping the law they continued in the covenant: their sanctification should be firm and perpetual if they walked in his commandments. And when it is added that all people of the earth should see the name of God called upon them, that is as much as to say it should be known that they were under God's defence and patronage, and so always safe and secure in his protection.
10:
Of the seeing and the fearing the notes are brief but not identical. Gill lists what the nations would see them called — his children, his people, his portion and his inheritance — and how the fact would be evident, by the care he took of them, the provision he made for them and the protection they had from him. Wesley makes it their being in truth his people and children, a most excellent and glorious people under the peculiar care and countenance of the great God. Ellicott gives the literal Hebrew instead, that the name of Jehovah has been called upon thee — a passive construction rather than the active one our version supplies — and matches the dread of the neighbours with the prophet's word that they shall fear and tremble for all the goodness and all the prosperity that God procures for Jerusalem. What the nations feel, on that reading, is awe at the evident favour rather than hostility toward its object.

On the plenty itself the three diverge again. Gill promises an affluence of all temporal good things, all things richly to enjoy, and once more reports the Targum of Jonathan substituting the Word of the Lord for the divine name, as it had done twice already in this passage. Ellicott corrects the English noun: not goods but good, or goodness — that is, prosperity, the same word the prophet uses of Jerusalem in the verse just cited. Wesley notices only that the same things said a few verses earlier are simply said over again, and reads the repetition as itself a part of the promise rather than an accident of style: God would repeat and multiply his blessings upon them, and the doubling of the words answers to the doubling of the gift.

Keil and Delitzsch look past all this to the figure the whole passage has been driving at, that by such blessings the Lord would make Israel the head and not the tail. The image, they say, is taken from life, and its meaning is obvious enough to need no explaining; they refer it to Isaiah, where the head and the tail are set for the elder and the honourable against the prophet that teacheth lies, and note that the sense given figuratively here is stated literally in the clause that follows it.
12:
What the treasure holds they settle from the clause after. Gill observes that the Lord has treasures of snow and hail and wind, but that his good treasure here is rain; Wesley calls it the heaven or air, God's storehouse, where he lays up rain or wind for use; Clarke names the clouds, so that fructifying showers descend at all requisite times and the vegetative principle in the earth exerts itself, making their crops abundant. Ellicott brings a Jewish saying here: there are three keys in the hand of the Holy One which he has not entrusted to a messenger — of the rains, of birth, and of the resurrection of the dead — and the proof text for the first is this very verse.

Calvin reads the rain as an argument about dependence. God's goodness shines in many ways, since he not only supplies the bread men eat but sends rain from heaven to water the earth, producing from his storehouse whatever is required for food; so let us learn, above and beneath — in the atmosphere, the sun's quickening heat, the rain, the earth's fertility — to contemplate the manifold riches God brings out of his treasures. From the promise to bless the work of our hands he draws the same lesson closer: we attain nothing by our industry and hardest labours except so far as God vouchsafes good success, all our efforts without his secret blessing being mere useless fatigue. Paul's figure for the culture of the Church is taken from nature itself — neither is he that planteth anything, neither he that watereth, but God that giveth the increase. God does not mean us to sit idle with our legs crossed like do-nothings; he requires the labour of our hands, but will have its fruit attributed to himself.

Then comes the difficulty the chapter invites. If all prosperity proceeds from the blessing God vouchsafes his servants, how is it that so many of his despisers have children, easy circumstances, abundance, honours and power? His answer is that the happy condition assigned to his servants does not prevent him diffusing his bounty promiscuously over the whole human race: he is called the preserver of man and beast, and Christ exalts his unbounded goodness in that he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good. Yet the prophet's exclamation is equally true, how great is thy goodness laid up for them that fear thee. God does good to the ungodly because he is their Creator; and to keep believers in suspense he suffers things to be confusedly mixed and hides his judgment as in the darkness of night, though he so tempers his patience that signs of his anger and favour appear even in the confusion. The faithful, not attaining the full enjoyment of the promise, taste it as far as is expedient; to the ungodly not a drop is dispensed, for unless a sense of his paternal favour is awakened by the blessing, the blessing ceases to exist. The more they gorge the more they attain a deadly fatness, and God lifts them up to cast them down more heavily, feeding them, as the prophet says, unto the day of slaughter. What God promises his own he seasons with spiritual salt, lest it be tasteless.

One difficulty remains, that this felicity does not always fall to God's servants, sharply tried even under the law. Since none was ever a perfect keeper of the law, Calvin answers, it is no surprise they enjoyed the promise only in part; and if they are chastised more severely than the ungodly, judgment usually begins at God's own house. Still the righteous are never forsaken, but are like green olive-trees in the courts of the Lord, while the ungodly, exalted a season like the cedars of Lebanon, are plucked up by the roots in a moment.
13:
Head and tail are read as rank rather than as parts of a body. Gill takes the promise for dominion over others rather than subjection to them, the head signifying rulers and governors and the tail the common people who are subjects — or, on another construction, the one honourable and in high esteem, the other mean and base — and once more notes the Targum of Jonathan's substitution of the Word of the Lord. Wesley makes the same point with a qualification: they should be chief of all people in power, or at least in dignity and privileges, so that even those not under their authority should reverence their greatness. It was so in David's and Solomon's time, he adds, and would have been so much oftener and much more if they had performed the conditions.

On the last clause the readings diverge over a point of grammar with a doctrine attached. Gill glosses going aside as departing from the words as a rule to walk by, turning out of them as a path to walk in, neglecting and disobeying them and going into practices contrary to them. Clarke makes the figure do the work: the way of obedience is a straight way and goes right forward, and he who declines either to right or left from that path goes astray and misses heaven. Ellicott raises the syntactical question. It is possible to attach the sentence to the condition in the verse before — if thou hearken and do not go aside — but the Septuagint, and apparently the Targums too, begin a fresh sentence here; and he thinks the second construction carries a thought quite at home in Jewish literature, that obedience begets obedience, the idea put so forcibly in the Revelation, that he which is unjust let him be unjust still, and he that is holy let him be holy still. Keil and Delitzsch look forward instead, and describe the shape of what is coming: after the announcement that all these curses would come upon the disobedient nation, the curse is proclaimed in its whole extent, covering every relation of life in a sixfold repetition of the word cursed, and the fulfilment of the threat in plagues and diseases, drought and famine, war, devastation and captivity is so depicted that the punishments stand out to view in ever increasing extent and fearfulness.
15:
Ellicott marks the hinge in a sentence: the verses from here to the end of the forty-eighth are the contrast to the first fourteen, which declared the blessings of obedience. Gill points back only to the hearkening the chapter has urged. Henry puts it as a turning of the cloud: having viewed the bright side, which is towards the obedient, we are now shown the dark side; and if we do not keep God's commandments we not only come short of the blessing but lay ourselves under a curse as comprehensive of all misery as the blessing is of all happiness. On the word overtake he and Wesley say the same thing in nearly the same words: the sinner shall not escape, though he vainly hope to, for there is no running from God but by running to him, no flying from his justice but by flying to his mercy.

Henry argues the equity of the sentence, this being no curse causeless nor for any light cause, since God neither seeks occasion against us nor is apt to quarrel with us. Three things bring it. Despising God, in refusing to hearken to his voice, bespeaks the highest contempt imaginable, as if what he said were not worth heeding. Disobeying him, in not doing his commandments or not observing to do them, is the second: none fall under his curse but those who rebel against his command. Deserting him is the third, the reason given later being the wickedness of their doings, whereby they had not only slighted God but forsaken him; and God never casts us off, Henry says, till we first cast him off. Of all their sins he expects idolatry to be the destroying one.

The extent he traces along the three lines the blessing had run. Wherever the sinner goes the curse follows: cursed in the city, whose strength cannot shelter him, and in the field, whose air is no fence against such pestilential steams; cursed coming in and going out, since he can neither leave it behind nor be rid of it, having taken it in like water and like oil into his bones. Whatever he has lies under it — the ground cursed for his sake and all that comes out of it, so that he is cursed from the ground as Cain was, while his basket and store, being forfeited, are forbidden him as cursed things, and embittered besides, since the wrath of God mixes itself with them. Whatever he does lies under it last, a constant disappointment in all he undertakes. The whole is the reverse of the blessing above: as whatever bliss there is in heaven there is in hell not only the want of it but the contrary to it — my servants shall eat, but ye shall be hungry.

Why the catalogue should be so long is Calvin's question, answered from the temper of the hearers. This list of curses is longer than the one proclaimed from Mount Sinai, because the Spirit of God foresaw that the sluggishness of the people had need of sharper stimulants; had they been moderately teachable, what they had already heard would have been more than enough to alarm them, but God redoubles his threatenings against their inertness, that they might not only fear but be roused by constant reminding. He notes the shape of the sixfold sentence that follows: cursed in city and field, at home and abroad; cursed in their food, in the seed and in the meal; and cursed in three kinds of fruit — their offspring, the produce of the soil and the young of their animals. Henry observes the like of the repetitions, that one judgment is threatened several times over to make the deeper impression, and to intimate that if men persist, the stroke they thought past will return with double force; for when God judges he will overcome.
16:
Here the sentence is simply the blessing turned over, and all three say so in their own way. Gill will not gloss the four verses at all, referring the reader back to what he had written on the corresponding promises: the curses are delivered out in form as the reverse of the blessings, and by observing what the blessings mean the sense of the curses may easily be understood, the one being directly opposite to the other. Keil and Delitzsch make the correspondence exact — these four verses answer precisely to the four that pronounced the blessing — and notice the one departure from the order, that the basket and the kneading-trough are named here before the fruit of the body, where in the blessing the children came first.

Calvin takes the last of the four and reads the merism in it. Going out and coming in signifies their various actions and the whole course of their life, so that what is pronounced is ill success upon every undertaking; and this, he says, is put more clearly still in the verse that follows, where God denounces misfortune in all their affairs, confounding and marring whatever they set their hand to. On the three Hebrew words gathered there he is content to leave the philology open. They are variously explained — one rendered vexation, or bruising and trampling and destruction; another rebuke, or reproach — and Keil and Delitzsch take them for synonyms strung together simply to strengthen the thought, the first meaning curse or malediction, the second the consternation such a curse produces, and the third a threatening or rebuke. Neither commentator will build anything on the distinction between the three, and Calvin says outright that they are variously explained. However they are parsed, Calvin says, the sum comes to the same: that God would be against them, so as to discomfit and overthrow all their counsels and labours.

From which he draws the lesson the blessings had already implied from the other side. If nothing prospers when God is against it, then all men's endeavours are useless and vain unless they seek their success from him.

Three words open the detailed sentence, and each is weighed. Gill takes the first either as a general term for all that follows or, since that has been said already, as a particular judgment, and reports Jarchi's reading of it as penury — want of all good things, extreme poverty, reduction to the utmost necessity, with their very blessings and mercies turned into curses. Clarke divides the three by their effects: cursing shall be their state, vexation the grief and trouble and anguish of heart, rebuke the continual judgments and marks of God's displeasure. Wesley locates the second in the mind, arising from the disappointment of hopes and from the presages of approaching misery, and takes the third to come from God not so much in words as by actions, by cross providences and sharp afflictions. Ellicott notices what our version hides, that all three nouns carry the definite article in the original, as though they were so many named diseases: the curse, and the terror, and the rebuke of the Almighty are terrible obstacles to any human undertaking. He renders the clause that follows literally, in every putting forth of thine hand which thou makest, and marks it as the exact reverse of the earlier blessing on the storehouses and on all that they set their hand to. On the last words of the verse he observes something characteristic of this book: Moses and Jehovah are here identified, for where the prophets say thus saith the Lord, Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, sometimes exhorts Israel in his own name without any such introduction — which is why apostasy from Moses could later be spoken of in the same breath as apostasy from God.
21:
The pestilence they all read from the verb. Gill notes it is not merely to come upon them but to continue with them; Clarke renders it that the Lord shall cement the plague to them, the Greek having it that he will glue and inseparably attach the death unto them, and adds that anyone who has heard the name can conceive how dreadful a plague must be that ravages without pause. Calvin generalises it: diseases are the lictors of God, and finally his executioners if men pertinaciously continue in their ungodliness, so that he does not merely say he will send the pestilence but will cause it to cleave, glued upon them till it consume them in the Holy Land itself. It is superfluous, he thinks, to speak particularly of the rest; only let us learn that while the multitude of diseases is almost innumerable, they are all so many ministers prepared to execute God's vengeance — and though they are contracted in various ways, especially by intemperance, this does not prevent God from smiting transgressors with them where no natural cause appears. Ellicott adds that the pestilence is one of the four sore judgments threatened against Jerusalem, and marks the range of what follows: through these verses we seem to be reading of the gradual consumption of Israel in the land of promise, before any actual captivity.

Clarke takes the catalogue word by word out of the Hebrew. The consumption is atrophy through lack of food; the fever a burning inflammatory one, from a root meaning to be kindled; the inflammation, from a verb meaning to pursue eagerly or burn after, probably a rapidly consuming cancer; the extreme burning is burning upon burning, scald upon scald, which he refers not only to inflammations of the body but to the agony of a mind utterly abandoned by God and lost to hope. The sword is war in general, enemies without and civil broils within, as was remarkably the case at the last siege of Jerusalem; the blasting either the blighting east wind or those pestilential winds that suffocate man and beast; the mildew an exudation of the vegetative juice by which the plant is kept from ever coming to maturity. Of the seven plagues, he counts, the first five fall on their bodies and the last two on their substance. Ellicott confirms the rarity of the words — consumption and fever occur only here and in the parallel curse in Leviticus, inflammation and extreme burning nowhere else — and glosses each from Rashi: the flesh consumed and puffed out, a heat greater than the fever, a disease that heats the body inwardly. Gill keeps to the plainest sense, an emaciation of the body through famine or wasting disease, till men are reduced to skin and bones.

The two blights Calvin treats separately, as the pair that destroy the corn just as it ripens and snatch the bread out of men's mouths: one an emptying of the ears caused by a dry east wind, the other when the sudden heat of the sun strikes corn still moistened with cold dew. Keil and Delitzsch add the drought that goes with them, a heaven of brass and an earth of iron, with dust and ashes falling instead of rain — the Hebrew making the rain of the land into dust and ashes — and explain it from the country itself, where in great heat the air is often full of dust and sand and the wind takes the form of a burning sirocco, so that the air resembles the glowing heat at the mouth of a furnace. Calvin will not let the natural explanation carry the whole weight. Although these evils arise from natural causes, God, the Author of nature, in his supreme power so controls the atmosphere that its unwholesomeness is his undoubted scourge, and a certain sign of his wrath.
23:
The two metals are read for hardness, not for shine. Gill says the heaven is like brass not for its clearness or splendour, as of a molten looking glass, but for its dryness and hardness, no moisture in it or passing through it. Clarke puts it in terms of the atmosphere, unreplenished with aqueous vapours, so that they had neither the early nor the latter rain, and the ground lay wholly intractable and incapable of cultivation; from which he draws the point of the image, that God shows himself Lord of nature, and that drought and sterility are not casualties but proceed from his immediate appointment. Ellicott adds a second turn of the screw: the brass and iron stand not only for the drought but for God's refusal to remove it, and he points to Jeremiah's intercession for Israel under this misery, answered by the order not to pray for this people for their good — grief permitted, relief withheld.

Calvin sets the threat against the promises it reverses. God, wishing to give a token of favour, often promises by the prophets the rain of autumn and of spring, the one following the sowing and the other giving growth before the fruits ripen, and in many places threatens to withhold them; that is what is meant here, since neither shall moisture descend to fertilize the earth, nor the earth, bound up and hardened, have juice or dampness for production. Whence we gather that not a drop of rain falls except as God distils it, and that whenever it rains the earth is irrigated as if by his hand — the more so because Canaan was not like Egypt, watered by the care and industry of man, but fertilized by the bounty of heaven. He notes that the words specify the heaven over our head and the earth under our feet, God's weapons being prepared above and below to assail the people on every side; and he sets beside it the chain in Hosea, where God reconciled will hear the heavens, and they the earth, and the earth the corn and the wine and the oil, so that at last all these shall hear starving men.

What falls instead of rain is read two ways, and Calvin gives both: either the rain shall fertilize the ground no more than ashes would, or dust shall fall in its place, as though God would dry up the rich soil by scattering ashes on it. Wesley allows the same two. Gill takes the second and explains the mechanism — the soil, parched and crumbled to dust, raised into the air by the force of winds and let down again in showers of dust, destroying what few herbs remain — and reports the Targum of Jonathan to the same effect; such ploughing winds, casting earth and sand into the air till men and cattle are covered, are frequent in the eastern countries. Clarke confirms it from travellers: whole caravans have been buried under showers of sand, and Thevenot, who observed such showers, says they grievously annoy all they fall on, filling the eyes and ears and nostrils. He thinks the ophthalmia of Egypt owing chiefly to a very fine sand whose particles are like broken glass. Ellicott needs a sentence: the great desert on Palestine's eastern frontier makes it only too possible.

Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the defeat that follows, the exact opposite of the blessing that had promised the enemy should flee seven ways. Israel would become what one Hebrew word calls a moving to and fro — a ball, so to speak, for all the kingdoms of the earth to play with — and they take some trouble over the form, arguing that this is not a later transposed spelling but the original uncontracted one, and the way the text should be read wherever this threat is repeated by the prophets.
25:
Gill dates the defeat rather than describing it, instancing the times Israel was smitten before the Philistines when they sinned, and afterwards by the Assyrians, Babylonians and Romans. Ellicott marks it as the contrary of the earlier promise, and takes up the word rendered removed: it is literally a removing, and the Greek here has the very word used in the New Testament for the dispersion, the scattered Israelites of the epistles — a threat repeated by Jeremiah for the sins of Manasseh.

Calvin reads the same verse for what it says about courage. What was briefly threatened under the name of the sword is now pursued at length, that they should be given up to the will of their enemies and indiscriminately slaughtered, the enemy conquering and pursuing them in flight. The detail he fastens on is the going out one way and the returning seven: they march out with their army in regular order and come back dispersed in all directions by the confusion of their flight. Hence the bravery of men is in God's power, so that he can make cowards of the boldest whenever he pleases — witness the question asked later, how should one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, except their Rock had sold them. For this reason God calls himself the God of hosts: that believers may live securely under his guardianship, while the despisers of the law dread the slightest motion when he is wroth. On being removed among all the kingdoms he reports two constructions — that they should be a laughing-stock, since we shake our heads by way of insult, or wanderers in unknown places of exile — and prefers the first, noting that Ezekiel uses the word for a tumultuous rout.

The unburied carcass is treated by all of them as a second death. Gill counts it a very grievous calamity to have no other burial than in the bowels of beasts and birds, as befell many in the Antiochian persecution, and cites a Jewish record of a persecution in Spain where those who fled were killed in the fields and left unburied. Ellicott finds the sentence repeated in Jeremiah, to be fulfilled in Tophet when there was no more room to bury; and on the clause that none should fray them away he recalls the one person in the histories who did that office — Rizpah, watching her children's bodies for half a year, suffering neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day nor the beasts by night. Here, he says, there shall be no one to do it.

Calvin explains why the want of a grave should count as a curse at all. The punishment is doubled by the disgrace added to the death, for it is ignominious to be deprived of burial, and a sign of God's paternal favour that we should be distinguished from the brutes, the rites of burial rousing us to the hope of resurrection; so God deprives of burial those whom he curses. Yet he enters the same caution he has entered before about bodily punishments, that they are common to the pious and the reprobate: the reprobate are sometimes honourably buried, as Christ relates of the rich man, while the bodies of the pious are ignominiously cast out to birds and beasts, as the psalmist complains. Such an interchange does not prevent God from avenging the contempt of his law in this way, as by pestilence, famine or sword. Keil and Delitzsch pass on to the diseases that follow, counting four incurable ones — the ulcer of Egypt, which they identify with elephantiasis, the leprosy peculiar to that country, differing from tubercular leprosy in degree only; and the tumour, a swelling the Rabbins take for a disease of the anus, the same the Philistines were smitten with.
27:
The botch of Egypt sets them hunting for a disease. Gill reports that some understand it of the leprosy, of the sort called elephantiasis, frequent among the Egyptians, and passes on two travellers' accounts of what the Nile does to the skin — Thevenot, that when the river's increase expires the Egyptians are attended with sharp prickings like needles, and Vansleb, that the waters cause an itch which begins about the arms, spreads next upon the stomach and then over the whole body with grievous pain, comes from cistern water as well as river water, and lasts about six weeks; though others, he adds, take the botch for the boils and blains the Egyptians were plagued with for refusing to let Israel go, which is Wesley's reading too. Clarke identifies it outright with elephantiasis and describes it at length as the most horrid disease that can afflict human nature: the whole body covered with a loathsome scurf, the joints preternaturally enlarged, the skin swelling and growing into folds like an elephant's — whence the name — and breaking across at every joint, with an abominable ichor flowing from the chinks; he refers the reader to Aretaeus for an account whose language, he says, is enough to chill the blood, and quotes Lucretius that the elephant disease is bred about the streams of the Nile, in mid Egypt, and nowhere else. Ellicott keeps to the philology, noting that the word is the same as the boil of the Egyptian plague, and quotes Rashi that it was very bad, being moist inside and dry outside; he adds that a learned Dalmatian Jew of his acquaintance had seen many such cases among the Hungarian and Polish Jews.

The three that follow are handled the same way. Clarke derives the emerods from a root meaning to be raised up — swellings or protuberances, probably the bleeding piles; finds the scab has no Hebrew verb behind it but an Arabic word for a distemper in the corner of the eye, which may amount to the Egyptian ophthalmia, though some suppose the scurvy; and makes the itch a burning one, something of the erysipelatous kind, commonly called St Anthony's fire. Ellicott identifies the emerods as haemorrhoids, notes that the scab is elsewhere rendered scurvy and would make both a priest and a victim unclean and unfit for the service of Jehovah, and glosses the itch from Rashi as a dry ulcer like a sherd. On the incurability both are exact in the same way: Clarke says that being inflicted by God's justice they could not be cured by human art, and Ellicott that it is not that these things are in themselves incurable, but that they should have them incurably. Calvin reads the whole clause historically. Whether the plagues meant are the extraordinary ones inflicted at the deliverance or the ordinary diseases that had prevailed in Egypt before — and he thinks the latter more probable — Moses signifies that while the Egyptians were smitten with them God's people escaped, a distinction that could not have happened naturally and so represented his favour the more clearly; the threat is that if they despise his law he will deal with them as they had seen him deal with heathen nations.
28:
Gill traces the madness to its occasion — the calamities that had befallen them, and the force of the diseases upon them. Keil and Delitzsch count three maladies of the mind here, and argue that the middle one is mental rather than bodily: though the word means primarily blindness of the eyes, its position between idiocy and confusion of the understanding points that way, as does the next verse, where Israel gropes in the bright noonday like a blind man in the dark and does not hit upon the road that leads to the goal. Clarke agrees the blindness is both physical and mental — the scab destroying their eyes, the judgments of God confounding their understandings — and gives the astonishment as stupidity and amazement, adding the old saying that those whom God is determined to destroy he first infatuates, and applying it, with some feeling, to the powers of Europe in his own day. Wesley reads blindness of mind, so that they should not know what to do, and astonishment as wonder and horror at the strangeness and soreness of their calamities. Ellicott only notes that all three words occur together in Zechariah, where the threat seems aimed at the enemies of Jerusalem rather than at Jerusalem itself.

Calvin thinks this the heaviest stroke in the list, though the least felt. The prophets very often speak of God smiting the wicked with a spirit of giddiness, making them drunk with astonishment; and from that blindness it comes that men rush wilfully into vile lusts, shudder at no crime, are hurried headlong to destruction, are deprived of discretion and throw away the remedies in their hands. The common apprehension of men is not greatly disturbed by this form of vengeance, and yet it is much more severe and awful than any bodily disease. The poets imagined that wicked men were agitated by the furies, because experience taught them that it was not without a secret impulse from God that they became so senseless, being in mind like beasts in the shape of men; so even the heathen perceived that when the wicked are given over to a reprobate mind, God is manifesting himself as the just avenger of their crimes. And so it is, Calvin ends, in every case of astonishment: those who are stupefied by their miseries are plainly prostrated by the hand of God.
29:
Groping at noonday is taken by all of them for a blindness of the mind. Gill argues from the comparison itself: to the blind, darkness and light are alike, so the force of saying at noonday is that what is meant is not the darkness of their bodily eyes but of their minds — unable to judge of things as clear as noon, at the utmost loss what method to take when the way is plain, and following instead the lusts and counsels of their own hearts. Wesley puts it in a line, that in the most clear and evident matters they should grossly mistake, and that their counsels and enterprises should be frustrated and turn to their destruction. Keil and Delitzsch take the same view and add the sense of not prospering — not hitting upon the right road that led to the goal and to salvation. Ellicott sets the clause against the promise to Joshua, that he should prosper if he followed the book of the law, and against Isaiah's sentence that the wisdom of their wise men shall perish and the understanding of their prudent men be hid. Clarke turns it on the history: perhaps no people under the sun have been more oppressed and spoiled, and this has been their portion with little intermission for nearly eighteen hundred years — and still they grope at noonday, not discovering, for all the light around them, that the rejection of their own Messiah is the cause of their calamities.

The plundering that follows is read by Calvin in an order of increasing pain. The most painful thing is put first, that they should be despoiled of their wives, the enormity magnified by making it not the wife torn from her husband's bosom but the betrothed virgin defiled. The denunciation extends next to houses and vineyards — grievous indeed to see the fruit of our labours seized before we have been permitted to enjoy it, since frustrated hope increases the pain; then to the flocks and herds; and then to the children, taken in their parents' very sight, so that their eyes should fail with grief and their hands, as if dead, be unable to help them. He gives two reasons why the robbers should be strangers unknown to them: that less consideration might be expected from barbarians than from neighbours, and that the Jews might be alarmed out of supposing they had only neighbouring nations to deal with, since it was in God's power to fetch nations from afar.

Gill fills in the first of these griefs from the custom of betrothal — a woman espoused in order to be made a wife, and before the marriage could be consummated set at a distance from him by some calamity and falling into another man's hands — which at that stage must be a grievous disappointment and a great vexation. Of the ox he says only that it would be taken from herd or stall by the enemy and killed for the soldiers to feed on, without the least part given back. Clarke will not pass the catalogue without a word to his own readers: can any heart imagine anything more grievous than to be on the brink of all domestic happiness and then suddenly deprived of it, and to see an enemy enjoy everything that was dear? They have grievously sinned, he grants, but have they not grievously suffered for it — and Christians should not, by unkind treatment, increase the miseries of the men who above all others have seen affliction by the stroke of his rod. Ellicott adds one exact note: where our version says none to rescue, the Hebrew is literally thou shalt have no saviour, and the times of oppression before the judges were raised up — who are themselves called saviours — must often have fulfilled the words for a season.
32:
Ellicott calls this verse perhaps the most pathetic piece of description in the whole chapter. Many of the nations bordering on Israel were accustomed, when they made inroads, to carry off not only the cattle but the children for slaves; and he sets beside it Jeremiah's voice heard in Ramah, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted because they were not — with the difference that it would not always be added, as it was there, that they shall come again from the land of the enemy. On the eyes failing he takes the verb for consuming, and quotes Rashi that all longing after what does not come is called a consumption of the eyes. The last clause he thinks very remarkable in the Hebrew: it means literally that thou shalt have no hand toward God, shalt not be able to lift a hand to him — and he compares Jacob wrestling with the angel, and Moses in the fight with Amalek, whose held-up hand made Israel prevail. Hezekiah could say mine eyes fail with looking upward; here the eyes fail with looking, but cannot look up.

Gill and Clarke both date the fulfilment late. Gill observes that this was not true of the Babylonish captivity, where sons and daughters went with their parents and returned with them, but has been verified often since the captivity by the Romans, their children taken by force to be brought up in another religion by edicts of kings and popes and by canons of councils. Clarke says the same of Spain and Portugal, where Jewish children were taken by order of government and educated in the Popish faith, and notes instances even in Protestant countries. Wesley reads it more plainly: children given or sold by their conquerors to others, eyes consumed partly with grief and partly with vain expectation of their return, and a hand with no power to rescue and no money to ransom.

Of the nation that should eat up their labour, Gill points to Jeremiah's prophecy of the Babylonish captivity as one fulfilment, and adds that it has been verified again in their present state, where, though they have no land to till, they are employed in manufactures and merchandise and have frequently been stripped of the fruit of both. Ellicott gives the parallel exactly — a nation whose language thou knowest not shall eat up thy harvest and thy bread — and Wesley draws out why the strangeness makes it worse: a nation from a far country, not expected or feared, and therefore the more dreadful when it comes; a nation whose language they do not understand, so that they can neither plead with them for mercy nor expect any favour.

The madness at the end is, for Gill, the sum of everything already threatened. It is not only the violent diseases, grievous to behold and intolerable to bear, but the loss of a betrothed wife, a new house and a new vineyard, the ox slain and the ass driven off and the sheep given to enemies before their eyes, the children taken and brought up in another religion, and the stripping of their substance — which have made men stark mad, so that they have sometimes destroyed themselves and their families. He gives two instances from Germany: a city burnt by its Jewish inhabitants with themselves in it, and a community summoned by edict to change their religion or burn, who met in one house to destroy one another, parents killing their children and husbands their wives before killing themselves. Wesley describes the state from within — men quite put out of the possession of their own souls, bereaved of comfort and hope and abandoned to despair — and draws the moral that those who walk by sight and not by faith are in danger of losing reason itself when all about them looks frightful.
35:
The botch in the knees is diagnosed more exactly than the earlier sores. Gill notes only that a sore in those parts is very painful and not easily cured, that this one was incurable by human art, and that it would not stop below but spread. Clarke and Ellicott identify it with the boil already named, Ellicott adding the prophets' phrase that all knees shall be weak as water. Keil and Delitzsch call it joint-leprosy, a form of the tubercular kind, but will not let the clause from sole to crown be restricted to that, since in leprosy of the joints the upper parts often remain normal. Moses names it, they think, as a disease making it impossible either to stand or walk, then heightens the threat by carrying it over the whole body — and they add what mattered most: leprosy excluded a man from fellowship with the Lord and deprived the nation of its character as a nation of God. Calvin sets it in a wider frame: since death is common to the race, all must be subject to sickness, and Adam's posterity, infected with sin, are liable to afflictions that are its wages; but because offences are not all alike, God keeps a just proportion in his punishments, and what is spoken of here is not common maladies but the incurable ones by which he openly shows his vengeance.

The captivity of the king is felt by all of them as the sharpest stroke yet. Gill finds it fulfilled in Jehoiachin and Zedekiah at Babylon. Ellicott counts more: Jehoahaz taken to Egypt, Jeconiah and Zedekiah to Babylon, and Hoshea, whose fate Scripture does not record, apparently taken with Samaria by the Assyrians. He argues from a silence besides: this is not the only place where Moses shows foreknowledge of a king, and could any later writer have concealed that there were two kingdoms, or avoided all allusion to the throne of David? Keil and Delitzsch supply the logic: the loss of their spiritual character would be followed by the dissolution of the covenant fellowship, which connects this verse to the leprosy.

Calvin reads it as the prophecy they found least credible. Its fulfilment taught the Jews, too late, that this was no empty threat; being so far off, they would never have supposed the Assyrians and Chaldeans to be God's scourges, and still less believed that the king they had themselves appointed should be dragged a prisoner into distant countries — a formidable punishment, since all their safety depended on their kingly government. He quotes Jeremiah magnifying that evil above the rest: the breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the Lord, was taken in their pits, of whom we said, under his shadow we shall live among the heathen. Let us learn, he says, not to measure God's judgments by our reason but to tremble at them though they are hidden. Wesley makes the point more briefly: the calamity is universal, since even the king cannot avoid it, and irrecoverable, since he who should rescue them is lost with them.

On serving wood and stone Calvin finds an aggravation and an irony together. They should be oppressed by such tyranny as to be compelled to serve wood and stone; dull as they were, they ought still to have abhorred such gross wickedness, from which it may be gathered that nothing but the terrible vengeance of God could have reduced them to it. For though they had run eagerly after the superstitions of the Gentiles, once deprived of the worship of God and put under that wretched servitude, the foulness of idolatry must have been more fully understood. An antithesis is implied: because they refused to submit to the true God, they should become the slaves of idols. Wesley says it in a sentence: what was formerly their choice and delight now becomes their plague.
37:
Being made a proverb is treated by all four as a distinct stroke, and not merely as a flourish upon the captivity just threatened. Gill puts it in terms of the neighbours, who should hear of their overthrow and captivity and see the miserable condition they were brought into — the astonishment being theirs, not Israel's, and the proverb and byword what they would make of it afterwards. Ellicott marks it as the exact contrary of the earlier promise that all the people of the earth should see the name of the Lord named upon them and be afraid, and observes that it was verified in the first captivity and did not wait for the last dispersion — the same threat having been repeated to Solomon at the dedication of the temple, and taken up afterwards by both Jeremiah and Ezekiel, who complains that the nations profaned God's holy name on account of it. Keil and Delitzsch add the mechanism, that the nation would be thrust into bondage among a people it did not know and become an object of disgust, a proverb and a byword to all nations whither God should drive it; and they treat the three words as one rising figure rather than three separate penalties.

Calvin calls this the climax of their miseries, and explains why a word should be counted worse than a wound. They should be so far from receiving consolation from men that on every side their misery would meet with taunts and insults; and nothing more bitterly wounds the wretched than this indignity of being harassed by reproaches and sarcasms, so that to be a laughing-stock and byword to all nations is a dreadful infliction. He finds an antithesis implied in it besides, between the ignominy to which God now condemns his ungrateful people and the extraordinary dignity with which he had honoured them, that they should be illustrious before the whole world. It is the promise of the first fourteen verses turned inside out: the nation that was to have been set on high above all nations of the earth is now to be pointed at by them. The prophets, Calvin notes, have often imitated this manner of speaking, in passages so common that he declines to quote any of them.
38:
Gill fixes the reference before anything else: these verses and those following plainly concern Israel while still in their own land, before the captivity, and not their present circumstances — a man sowing his field plentifully and expecting a harvest, planting vineyards and dressing them in expectation of much fruit, owning olive trees through all the coasts of a country that is called for that reason a land of olive oil. On the last of the losses he is briefest: they shall beget sons and daughters and yet these shall not be theirs, being taken from them and given to others.

Calvin reads the sequence as a set of different causes for one scarcity. The harvest shall be scanty notwithstanding an abundant sowing, because the locust consumes the seed; the vintage poor, and almost nothing, because the worms devour the bunches; the oil little, because the olives wither on the trees and fall of themselves. By which God admonishes them that he has innumerable ministers at hand to destroy the transgressors of his law by famine. Whenever we see beetles and locusts and other insects attacking the fruits, Calvin says, we should remember that God is as it were putting forth his arm to take away the food he had given — as Joel reminds us, that when the locust eats what the palmerworm has left, and another insect what the locust has left, God's hand is quite evident. Philosophers can discover why more of these little creatures are generated in one year than another; but we must hold to the teaching of Moses, that they never trouble us except by God's command. If we were as submissive to God as we ought to be, no such prodigy would ever happen as that vile and filthy insects should devour the fruits of the earth which he himself provided for the sustenance of his children.

Keil and Delitzsch keep to the words. The olive is not merely to be barren: the verb means it would be rooted out or plundered, and they argue the form against the alternative parsing that would make it drop its fruit of itself. The sons and daughters would be begotten but not kept, because they would have to go into captivity. And the creature named at the end they call the buzzer, from a root meaning to buzz, a rhetorical epithet for the locust rather than for the grasshopper — since a grasshopper does not injure the fruits of tree or ground enough for the strong verb used here, which means to take possession of, to be applicable to it. Gill describes the same insect from its effects, one that consumes not only grass and herbs and the corn of the field but green trees as well, and derives its name either from the shade such swarms make, hiding the light of the sun and darkening the face of the earth at noonday, or from the noise they make with their wings in flying.

Keil and Delitzsch look ahead from here to the reversal that follows, where the stranger within Israel rises very high and Israel itself sinks very low. They reject the explanation that the stranger prospers because, having no landed possession, he depended on resources of another kind; the reason, they think, is simply that he and all his possessions would be exempted from the curse of God — as the Israelites had themselves been exempted from the plagues that fell on the Egyptians.
43:
The reversal turns on who is the guest. Wesley catches it in a phrase — the stranger within thy gates, who formerly honoured and served thee, and some of whom were glad of the crumbs that fell from thy table. Gill spells out what the rising means: above them in wealth and riches, in power and authority, in honour and dignity, so that one who had been a stranger or a proselyte of the gate while they were in their own country should now stand vastly above them; and he reports that Manasseh Ben Israel referred the words to the Samaritans, whom the king of Assyria settled in and about Samaria — though Gill takes the design of the expression to be simply how mean and abject Israel should become in another country. On the lending he is careful about what the verse is and is not saying: the point is that the stranger should be in a capacity to lend when the Jew, his circumstances being so low, would not be able to lend to the Gentile, and it is meant to show the change of condition, not the kindness or unkindness of either party.

Keil and Delitzsch give the same reading in a sentence, that what happens here is the exact opposite of the two promises earlier in the chapter, that Israel should lend to many nations and not borrow, and should be the head and not the tail. On why the stranger in particular should thrive they will not accept the explanation that he prospered because, owning no land, he depended on other kinds of resources; the reason is rather that he and all his possessions would be exempted from the curse of God, in the same way that the Israelites had been exempted from the plagues that fell upon the Egyptians. They also mark where the address is going: at the next pause it returns to its own beginning, with the threat that these curses shall be upon thee for a sign and a wonder, and upon thy seed for ever — a sign and wonder because their magnitude and terrible character manifest so clearly the supernatural interposition of God. The for ever they restrict to the generation smitten by the curse, which would remain for ever rejected, without that involving the perpetual rejection of the whole nation, or making impossible the conversion and restoration of a remnant, or of a holy seed.

Calvin reads the debt itself as the proof. That the sojourners who dwelt in Canaan on sufferance should in a manner become its masters was no doubtful mark of God's wrath, since we know how far those in debt are under the power of their creditors, and Solomon's saying is found true, that the rich ruleth over the poor and the borrower is servant to the lender. The Israelites must have felt God was against them when they became suppliants to their own guests, especially since he had promised to enrich them so that they should lend to others; that revolution of affairs plainly convicted them of their iniquities.

He enters his usual caution alongside it. Poverty as well as wealth is in God's hands, and while wealth is a proof of his favour and poverty reckoned among his curses, it remains true that God often chastises his own children with want, or proves and exercises their patience, without ceasing to be their Father — while he bestows abundance on the reprobate for them to gorge themselves to their own destruction. Still, God's blessing does shine forth in the elect so far as it is expedient for them; nor is it said in vain in the psalm that wealth and riches are in the house of the just, and said there for a reason: that he may lend, and be bountiful.
45:
Gill only gathers the reference: all these curses means those already related as well as those that follow. Calvin reads the verse as closing every exit. It takes away all hope of alleviation, since God's scourges shall not cease until the people have repented. All the curses shall come; for though they are not always gathered into a single band, God pays the wages of transgressors with the whole multitude of miseries Moses has recounted. The word pursue takes away all hope of escape, and overtake is laying hold of them tenaciously, till, as it is further said, they are destroyed. The sum is that the ungodly, by their subterfuges, only accumulate heavier punishments on themselves, which never cease to afflict them until they perish under them. Ellicott qualifies the last word: destroyed does not mean exterminated, the root being connected with smiting and the idea rather to crush — as when the king of Syria is said to have destroyed Israel and made them like the dust by threshing.

Why they should be a sign and a wonder Calvin explains from the effect on the onlooker: they shall awaken astonishment in all men, for those little moved by God's common judgments are compelled, whether they will or no, to attend to prodigies. He notices what is reproved besides their contempt of the law — their ingratitude, that they served not God with joyfulness of heart when he had been so generous to them; for it is the fault of a corrupt nature that it cannot be brought to serve God joyfully when he invites us by his liberality. Keil and Delitzsch describe the motive behind the passage: though every side of the national life has already been brought under the curse, love to his people and the desire to preserve them from it impel the faithful servant of the Lord to go further still, and depict more minutely the horrors of Israel's being given up to the heathen.

Where the prophecy lands is Wesley's and Henry's concern. Wesley thinks Moses has been foretelling the Babylonish captivity until now, and that from here he foretells the last destruction by the Romans; the present deplorable state of the Jewish nation answers the prediction so exactly that it is an incontestable proof of the truth of the prophecy and of the divine authority of the Scriptures. Henry traces the same history: plucked from off the land not only by the Babylonish captivity and the Roman destruction of Jerusalem but afterwards, when they were forbidden to set foot in the city; no rest of body, continually on the remove in hope of gain or fear of persecution, and no rest of mind, which is much worse; banished from city to city and country to country, recalled and banished again. It is amazing, he says, that a people so long the favourites of heaven should be so cast off, and yet that a people scattered among all nations should be kept distinct.

Two conclusions Henry draws. The first is evidential: the accomplishment of these predictions shows that Moses spoke by the Spirit of God, who foresees the ruin of sinners and warns them of it, that they may prevent it by a true and timely repentance or else be left inexcusable. The second is a warning: we should learn to stand in awe and not to sin, for if we will not fear God's fearful name we shall feel his fearful plagues, one way or other God being determined to be feared. Yet these miseries are but the beginning of sorrows to those under God's curse; and Henry closes where the chapter cannot, by turning to the remedy: let us be thankful that Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us and bearing in his own person the punishment we must otherwise have endured for ever.
46:
Gill turns the sign and the wonder into an argument. The curses were to rest and remain upon them, continuing and very visible, so as to be observed by others as a sign of God's displeasure, of the fulfilment of prophecy, and of the truth of divine revelation; and a wonder, because it is astonishing to observe how exactly the things threatened have fallen upon them and abode with them, in their former captivities and more especially in the present one. What he finds the greater wonder is the survival: that notwithstanding calamities so dreadful and so long continued, enough to have crushed any people from being a people, they have continued and still continue a distinct people — a standing miracle, and one he thinks sufficient to convince the most hardened deist of the authority of the Scriptures, in which stand so many prophecies fulfilled and continually fulfilling in this people. Wesley presses the same paradox from the other side: it is amazing that a people so incorporated should be so universally dispersed, and that a people scattered among all nations should mix with none of them, but, like Cain, be fugitives and vagabonds and yet so marked as to be known.

The reason given for it all is read by everyone as an exchange of services. Gill puts the failure plainly, that they did not serve the Lord by attending his worship and keeping his commandments; and therefore, since they would not serve so good a master, who supplied them with all good things in plenty, they should serve other lords — their enemies, whom God would raise up and send against them, not only Assyrians, Chaldeans and Babylonians but the Romans afterwards, whom they should find hard masters. Clarke says the same in a sentence: because they would not serve God, they became slaves to men.

Keil and Delitzsch put the weight on the two adverbial clauses. It was because Israel had not served the Lord its God with joy and gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things — that is, for the abundance of the blessings its God had bestowed on it — that it would serve its enemies in hunger and thirst and nakedness and want of everything, and wear an iron yoke, obliged to perform the hardest tributary service until it was destroyed. The contrast, on their reading, is not merely between serving God and serving men, but between serving in plenty with a glad heart and serving in destitution under a yoke.
49:
Which nation is meant divides them, and the phrase from the end of the earth forces the question. Gill grants that Babylon is called a nation from far, but denies it was ever from the end of the earth; and though Rome itself lay no great distance from Jerusalem, the emperors and much of the armies brought against the city were fetched from Britain, once reckoned the end of the earth. He cites Manasseh Ben Israel for referring the nation to Rome, and for the note that Vespasian brought many soldiers out of England, France and Spain; and adds that when the Jews rebelled under Adrian, Julius Severus, an eminent general, was likewise called from Britain to quell them. It is an ancient Jewish opinion, he says, that Rome is meant. Clarke agrees and adds two proofs: the eagle was the very animal borne on all the Roman standards, and the tongue not understood is the Latin, than which no language was more foreign to the idiom of the Hebrew.

Ellicott and Calvin hold out for the Chaldeans, on the ground of the prophet who quotes the words. Ellicott sets beside it Jeremiah's threat of a mighty and ancient nation from far, whose language thou knowest not — that bitter and hasty nation of Habakkuk — and grants only that the eagles of Rome may be alluded to, since of the Chaldeans too it is said that they shall fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat. On the unintelligible tongue he adds an observation of his own day, from a learned Jewish friend: excellent linguists as the Jews often are, hundreds never attain the least acquaintance with the language of the countries where they are dispersed, and seem to lose the power of doing so; not from lack of ability, he thinks, but from a paralysis of the understanding outside a certain range of thought.

Calvin reads the strange language as the cruellest detail of the threat. Unknown and barbarous enemies should attack with great impetuosity, and their cruelty is aggravated by their speech, for where there can be no oral communication there is no room for entreaties, which sometimes awaken even the savage to mercy. He too finds the fulfilment in the Chaldeans by Jeremiah's words, and notices that Isaiah, promising deliverance, counts among the chief blessings that the Jews should not hear a people of deeper speech than they could perceive, of a stammering tongue they could not understand. The prophets, he observes, took their very form of expression from Moses, lest the Jews should after their custom proudly despise threats God had interwoven with his law. And lest the distance of those countries lull them into security, the enemy is made swift as eagles, to overwhelm them suddenly — as God often compares the ministers of his wrath to the whirlwind, and as Jeremiah imitated the figure when he declared that the slaughter the Jews imagined far off should come upon them at once.

Of the fierce countenance Gill says strong of face aptly describes the old Romans, as the Chaldeans are called a nation dreadful and terrible and the fourth beast a terror to all the world. Ellicott illustrates the want of respect for age and youth from the chronicler, where the king of the Chaldees had no compassion on young man or maiden or him that stooped for age, and from the Lamentations, where the faces of elders were not honoured. Keil and Delitzsch describe what such a foe leaves: it would consume all the fruit of cattle and land, everything gained by agriculture and the breeding of stock, until the nation was utterly destroyed, and would besiege it in all its gates till the lofty fenced walls it trusted in came down. Gill spells out the cattle as larger and lesser, oxen and sheep with their calves and lambs and kids.
52:
Gill takes the gates for their cities and walled towns, which had gates and bars for security. Clarke names the besiegers and the manner: Nebuchadnezzar first and Titus afterwards, who should beset them round on every side and cast a trench about them, lines of circumvallation such as our Lord predicted; and the words in all thy gates throughout all thy land show that the subjugation would be complete, since not Jerusalem only but every fortified place should be taken — which was done literally by the Chaldeans and the Romans alike. Ellicott supplies an instance from each side of that history: Jeremiah's mention of the last two fenced cities still besieged by Nebuchadnezzar's army, and the siege and capture of Jotapata by the Romans, recorded specially by Josephus, in spite of all the efforts of the Jews to defend it.

Calvin reads the verse as the demolition of a false confidence. The number of their towns inspired them with courage, since they never would have supposed that enemies would undergo so much fatigue as to keep fighting until every one was taken; and so all their towns are included, in whose multitude they had trusted when they despised any hostile aggression. He adds that their trust in high and fortified walls is equally vain, and allows the clause to be explained two ways — that the enemy should overthrow and lay their fortresses prostrate with military engines, or that the walls, however high, should be passed over by sheer perseverance, the towns surrendering from the mere length of the siege. Both, he thinks, are indicated, the enemy's valiant fighting and his patience. The repetition at the end magnifies the evil: they should be pressed so sorely in their own land, the land God had given them, and the very associations of the place increased the indignity.

What the siege drives them to Gill will not describe beyond saying that nothing can be more shocking and unnatural. Ellicott points to where it was fulfilled — the siege of Samaria by the Syrians, and Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar, where the Lamentations twice record it. Keil and Delitzsch mark it as the refrain of what follows, the words about the siege and the straitness returning with their appalling sound through the verses after.

Calvin treats it as the worst of the portents, and explains why.
