It is an act of ferocity detestable and more than tragical that fathers and mothers should eat their own offspring, the love of which is so naturally implanted in every heart that parents often forget themselves in their anxiety for their children, and many have not hesitated to die to secure their safety; when even the brute animals cherish their young so carefully, what can be more disgusting than that men should cease to care for their own blood? Yet the threat by no means failed of fulfilment. We ought to be the more alarmed, he says, when we see that God punished so terribly the sins of those whom he had deigned to choose for his own — though not without just cause, since the Jews had left no kind of iniquity undone. Never must it be forgotten that those of the household of the Church, to whom God's truth is revealed, are on that account the less excusable, since they provoke his wrath knowingly and willingly. The brutality is heightened still further, he adds, by the persons: men in other respects tender and accustomed to delicacies should be so savage through hunger as to refuse a share of this horrible food to their own wives and surviving children — as Jeremiah says expressly that the pitiful women should be so maddened by hunger as to cook their own children.
54:
The horror is located in the persons chosen, and everyone notices it. Gill points out that the man instanced is not the rustic brought up meanly and used to hard living, but one bred tenderly who had fared sumptuously every day; and the woman is instanced because of her sex, the more pitiful and compassionate, and because she had been brought up genteelly and used to all the delights of nature. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same delicacy from the Hebrew, the woman who had never attempted to set her foot to the ground, having always been carried on a litter or an ass. The evil eye they gloss as looking with envy or ill-favour on the brother, the wife of the bosom and the remaining children, so as not to give them any; Wesley makes it unkind, envious and covetous to monopolise these dainty bits, grudging that the dearest relations should have any part of them, and of the woman that she would desire or design their destruction for her food. Ellicott sums the structure: a complication of horrors, in which they eat some of their children and then refuse to share even that food with those left. Gill says the same of the man who will give neither brother nor wife nor surviving child the least bit of what he has dressed for himself.

On the young one that cometh out from between her feet the versions divide. Gill takes it for the secundine or afterbirth, following the Targum of Jonathan and Aben Ezra, who describes it as the place of the foetus while it abides in the womb — and the suggestion is that, nauseous as it is, the delicate woman should eat that, and then the newborn child wrapped in it, though Jarchi understands the phrase of little children. Clarke sees a species of tautology in the two clauses and removes it by rendering the word literally as her secondines, which he says is the meaning of the Arabic, not badly understood by the Septuagint and still better by Luther as the after-birth. So read, it marks the deepest distress, the mother feeling the most poignant regret that her child was brought forth into such suffering and death, and being likely herself to survive the birth. He reports Kennicott's emendation besides — a change of one word making the clause read she shall boil that which cometh out from between her feet, even her children — which would match the prophecy to the two women of Samaria who agreed to eat their own children, the very same verb being used there; but he sees no absolute need of it.

Where it was fulfilled the two commentators who name it agree. Clarke says it was literally fulfilled when Jerusalem was besieged by the Romans, in the case of a woman named Mary, of a noble family, who, driven to distraction by famine, boiled and ate her own child, with a similar case in the siege of Samaria; Ellicott names her Mary of Beth-ezob and points to the story told with horrible minuteness by Josephus and again by Eusebius in his Church History — adding that the secrecy of the deed was one of its horrors, which is the very thing the verse specifies. Keil and Delitzsch mark the turn that comes next: these calamities would still not be the end of the distress, since the full measure of the curse was to be poured out only when Israel's disobedience had hardened into disregard of the glorious and fearful name of the Lord its God, which is why the resistance of the people is described in the verses following not as failing to hearken to a voice but as failing to observe the words written in this book.
58:
Gill identifies the book first — this book of Deuteronomy, in which the laws before delivered are repeated and some new ones added. Calvin fastens on the same phrase and on its severity. Even believers, though disposed to a willing obedience and earnestly applying themselves to the law, are impeded by the infirmity of the flesh; so what is demanded here is care and attention, since to observe to do is equivalent to giving sedulous and diligent heed. It is a harsh threat that leaves transgression in any respect without remission, for perfect obedience is required by the words all the words that are written; but Moses was thus severe, Calvin says, so that the people, convinced of their condemnation, should betake themselves to God's mercy — since no one longs after Christ until he first abandons all confidence in his works and rests his whole hope on gratuitous pardon. The curse so awaits transgressors that God pardons his children while sometimes chastising them, and executes on the reprobate the vengeance they deserve.

The clause about fearing the name Calvin takes for the fountain-head of the whole: all virtues are but smoke which do not spring from the fear of God, and the name is called glorious and fearful expressly so that contempt of it should be without excuse, it being gross stupidity, when God's majesty is openly set before us, not to be affected with becoming reverence. Ellicott sets the promise and the threat side by side on the diseases: against the word in Exodus that if they hearkened diligently God would put none of the diseases of Egypt upon them, for he is Jehovah that healeth thee, stands the word in Ezekiel that they shall know he is Jehovah that smiteth — the healer and the smiter being one Jehovah.

On the word rendered wonderful the readings converge with a difference of emphasis. Gill glosses the plagues as visible, remarkable, distinguishable and astonishing to all who see them. Keil and Delitzsch render it that the Lord would make the strokes of Israel and of its seed wonderful, that is, would visit them with extraordinary strokes, great and lasting, and with evil and lasting diseases. Calvin reports that some construe the verb as separating and others as increasing wonderfully, but thinks both too constrained; the root means to be wonderful, or secret and hidden, and what is meant is extraordinary modes of vengeance surpassing the comprehension of the human mind. On the second epithet he is careful: the word rendered faithful may mean either that the plagues shall certainly occur or that they shall continue to the end, and he prefers the latter, so that continued duration is added to their greatness.

Why the diseases should be Egypt's in particular Calvin explains from what the people had watched rather than suffered. These are not the diseases they had themselves undergone in Egypt but those under which they had seen the Egyptians labouring; so the threat is that the severity of God against unbelievers, of which they had been spectators, should fall on their own heads if they became followers of the same ungodliness — it being natural to tremble at judgments one has witnessed. Gill takes the same view, understanding either the plagues brought on the Egyptians for refusing to let Israel go or the diseases peculiar and common among them, the leprosy and the itch and ulcers. Keil and Delitzsch add the philological point that the verb means to turn back, since Israel had been set free from those diseases by the deliverance out of Egypt, and they distinguish the two classes named next: the diseases written in the law, which include the murrain, the boils and blains and the death of the firstborn, and the strokes, which are the rest of the plagues — the frogs, gnats, flies, hail, locusts and darkness.
61:
The open-ended clause here is what the commentators dwell on. Gill reads it as leaving nothing out: whatever sickness could be named, or was at any time in any place among men, might be expected to come upon them for their disobedience. Ellicott needs only the apostle's words — well might he write that it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. Calvin finds here a confirmation of his earlier point, that the sickness stands first as the particular and the plague follows as the wider term comprehending all the curses; and he draws out the force of the addition. After so many punishments have been enumerated, God declares he is armed with yet other weapons; and as his blessings are endless, so his power is incomprehensible for avenging the contempt of his law. Posterity has experienced how true these threatenings were, and we perceive it still, for as men's obstinacy has burst forth more and more, so new and unheard-of punishments have abounded from God like a deluge.

On the reduction of their numbers Gill supplies the histories. Very few were left in Judea when Jerusalem was taken, and those of the poorer sort, kept for vinedressers; and how far the Romans reduced them appears from Josephus, who reckons eleven hundred thousand slain at the siege and ninety-seven thousand made prisoners, the whole destroyed in the nation being computed above a million and a quarter. He adds from a Jewish historian that of those transported into Spain scarce a thousandth part remained, that an infinite number were slain in France and Germany, and that though their number had equalled those who came out of Egypt, scarce five thousand were left.

Calvin will not let the comparison be read as rhetoric about many and few. Since it had been promised to Abraham that his seed should be as the stars for multitude, their reduction to a handful was a signal token of God's wrath; so the comparison must be referred not simply to the great band and the small number but to the promise itself — that they might perceive that their former populousness could only have been ended, like waters dried up by the sun's excessive heat, through the wrath of God. Keil and Delitzsch say the same in a phrase: Israel would be almost annihilated, left a small number where it had been as numerous as the stars.

The hardest sentence in the chapter, for Keil and Delitzsch, is the one about God's pleasure. The Lord would find his pleasure in the destruction of Israel as he had rejoiced in blessing and multiplying it; and by that bold anthropomorphism Moses seeks to remove the nation's last prop of false confidence in the mercy of God. Greatly as man's sin troubles God, and little as his pleasure is in the death of the wicked, the holiness of his love demands the punishment of those who despise the riches of his goodness, so that he displays his glory in judgment no less than in blessing the righteous. Wesley presses the hard half rather than softening it: God's indignation will be so great that it will be a pleasure to him to take vengeance, for though he does not delight in the death of a sinner in itself, he delights in glorifying his justice upon incorrigible sinners, the exercise of all his attributes needing to please him. Gill lets the first half of the antithesis do the work, listing what the rejoicing to do good had consisted of: he brought them out of Egypt with great delight and pleasure in them, conducted them through the wilderness, protected them and provided all good things, brought them into a land flowing with milk and honey and settled them there, and gave them judges and kings, priests and prophets, for a long series of time.
64:
Calvin reads these verses as a descent by steps. Banishment had been threatened just before, and that was far more painful to Israel than to other nations: affection for one's country is natural to all, but their case was peculiar, since Canaan had been promised them by God, and they could not be expelled without being renounced by their heavenly Father. Now a second and a third step are added — to banishment a miserable scattering, and to scattering a trembling full of disquiet. Had they been driven together into one corner of the world their exile would have been more tolerable for the very association; the calamity is augmented when the storm of God's wrath scatters them like chaff into widely different countries. A further servitude comes in by the way, that he would enslave them not only to men but to idols. The third step is the want of rest — the most wretched state of all, to serve tyrannical conquerors and yet have no certain master; a just reward, he adds, of men who had rejected the rest God offered them.

Gill and the rest confirm each part from the history. On the scattering Gill notes their present dispersion, more or fewer in all parts of the world; Clarke says how literally it has been fulfilled, the people scattered over every nation under heaven. On serving other gods Ellicott is careful: we do not know of Israel falling into actual idolatry in dispersion, except in Egypt and possibly Babylon — but they were slaves to the worshippers of other gods. Keil and Delitzsch put the homelessness plainly: banished among the nations, Israel would find no rest for the sole of its foot — no place where it could set its foot down and have peace in its heart — and to that a trembling heart, failing of the eyes, and despair of soul. Gill lists the machinery of it — cruel edicts, heavy fines, exorbitant taxes, the searches of the courts of inquisition where any substance was to be got — and observes that the Jews themselves own the passage fulfilled in them. Ellicott calls the persecutions of the dispersion among the most fearful and wonderful phenomena of history, and glosses the failing eyes from Rashi as looking for salvation and it cometh not — asking how many years they have prayed to keep the feast next year in Jerusalem while the hope is deferred. Clarke reads the same clauses as insecurity under every government and an ever-disappointed expectation of the Messiah; Wesley has them tossed from place to place and sold from person to person, or wandering like Cain.

Calvin will not let this fear pass as a light matter, and enlarges it because the fear of spiritual punishments affects ungodly men so little. It is sadder to be agitated within by secret fear than oppressed by outward violence; for believers, though tossed by many waves, repose with tranquil minds on God, while the wicked, however they desire to lull themselves in security, are never truly at peace. He illustrates it from Dionysius, who had an exquisite supper prepared for the flatterer who had praised his happiness, set him in his own seat, and hung a sword above his head by a thread, so that the man who had called the tyrant happy, seeing death that near every moment, dared taste neither meat nor drink — whereby Dionysius confessed, not without shame, that tyrants are tormented by perpetual fear while they are formidable to others. The same disquiet is common to all despisers of God: the more wantonly they rage in forgetfulness of his fear, the more deservedly they dread their own shadow. Tranquillity of mind, Calvin concludes, can only arise from having God as our keeper; and by the sight of thine eyes he understands the spectres by which death is set before the reprobate.
66:
Of the life hanging in doubt Keil and Delitzsch give the figure exactly: it will be like some valued object hanging by a thin thread before the eyes, which any moment might tear down, so that a man despairs of preserving it and cannot believe in his own life from one hour to the next. They set beside the verse a remark of Luther's, that he had never seen a passage which describes more clearly the misery of a guilty conscience, in words and thoughts so fitting and appropriate, since this is just the way a man is affected who knows that God is offended, and who is harassed with the consciousness of sin.

Where the danger comes from the others divide, and between them they cover both sides. Gill keeps it outward and simple — the doubt is whether the enemy will spare the life or not, a man's continuance depending on another man's mercy. Wesley allows either cause: that they are in the hands of enemies who have the power and want no will to destroy them, or that the terrors of their own mind and the guilt of conscience make them fear even where no fear is. Ellicott quotes Rashi for the thought as the man himself would frame it: perhaps I shall die to-day by the sword that cometh upon me.

On the wish that runs between morning and evening they are agreed and add little to each other. Gill imagines the man wishing he may get through the day well, fearing his life will be taken before night or some sad calamity befall him before the day is past. Keil and Delitzsch put both halves together: in the morning they would wish it were evening, and in the evening wish it were morning, from a perpetual dread of what each day or each night would bring. What makes the alternation is named in the verse itself, and neither commentator softens it — the fear of the heart wherewith they should fear, and the sight of the eyes which they should see. The dread, that is, is not of any one calamity but of whatever the next hour happens to hold, so that neither light nor darkness can be wished for without wishing at once to be out of it.
68:
Keil and Delitzsch say why this is kept for last: Moses mentions the worst, the return to Egypt into ignominious slavery, for if the exodus was the birth of the nation of God, its return would be its death. In ships means in a way that cut off escape; and the clause following is not, they insist, an explanation of the ships, since Israel had not come out of Egypt by sea but by land through the desert. It serves only to strengthen the threat, that God would make them take a road they would never have seen again had they kept their dependence on him.

Calvin makes the same distinction. It was most to be desired by their posterity that they should never be carried back into that wilderness, where their fathers had been so driven about that they escaped only by extraordinary miracles; to bring them back was in a manner to blot out the grace of redemption. If any object that a people could not be conveyed in ships through dry places, the reply is easy: captivity being what is spoken of, there is no absurdity in their being carried by sea and set ashore. Wesley reads the words the same way — not the land road from Canaan but the end of the journey, Egypt itself — and adds the stroke that gives the phrase its edge: it seems meant to remind them of the time they went over the sea without ships, God drying it up before them, which they would now sadly remember.

On the fulfilment they are circumstantial. Gill will not refer it to the flight into Egypt after Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem, that being against God's express command; and though thousands went thither after the sedition in Syria, and Ptolemy Philadelphus set free a hundred and twenty thousand slaves, what is chiefly meant is their case under the Romans, when Titus sent all above seventeen to the works in Egypt. Clarke and Ellicott say the same from Josephus; Calvin adds from Aristeas that Egypt was the great slave-mart of antiquity, and Wesley that multitudes were carried thither and sold.

The last clause is strangest, and they read it three ways. Clarke takes the verb as exposing oneself for sale, the people being vagrants who wished to be slaves for the sake of necessaries — and no man would buy, since even the Romans thought it a reproach to have a Jew for a slave. Wesley allows two reasons: either the captives should be so many that the market would be glutted, or so loathsome and contemptible that none would have them; and he too appeals to Josephus for their state after the destruction of Jerusalem. Ellicott reports Rashi's reading — that they shall desire to be sold, offering themselves and being refused because appointed to slaughter, or that sellers shall pass them to other sellers and none care to keep them — but prefers the word as Nehemiah uses it of brethren redeemed from the heathen: they shall be sold to their enemies and none will redeem them.

Two close the chapter rather than the verse. Clarke calls it an astonishing chapter, containing prophecies delivered three thousand years ago and now fulfilling, and asks what proof it affords of the divine origin of the Pentateuch; he adds that in the most correct Hebrew Bibles the first verse of the next chapter is counted as the last of this one, a new subject beginning only afterwards. Wesley ends with a story he had heard: let us learn to stand in awe and not to sin, for he had heard of a wicked man who, reading these threatenings, was so enraged that he tore the leaf out of his Bible — but to what purpose deface a copy while the original remains unchangeable, by which it is determined that the wages of sin is death.
